original.guitar: Nashville session players (not credited in the sources found); Telecaster-style twang
original.amp: Unknown. Typical modern-country clean: Fender-style amp, compressed
original.effects: Compressor, slapback delay, spring reverb (genre style, not documented)
original.notes: From This One's for You (2017), produced by Scott Moffatt. No source documents the gear, so this tone follows the style of the record.

recipes.tips: Channel A for the clean, twangy fills and chicken-pickin' licks: hybrid-pick (pick plus middle finger) close to the bridge. Switch to channel B for a gritty tweed edge when the band kicks in. The compressor and the 120 ms slapback are what make it sound country, so keep them on.
recipes.why: Modern country electric parts are usually a Telecaster bridge pickup into a clean Fender-style amp, squashed by a compressor, with a short slapback. Pulled (split) Pearly Gates on the bridge is the closest your guitar gets to a Tele bridge pickup.

original.guitar: Nashville session players (not credited in the sources found)
original.amp: Unknown. Typical modern-country rock crunch: Marshall-style amp
original.effects: Light overdrive, delay, room reverb (genre style, not documented)
original.notes: From This One's for You (2017), produced by Scott Moffatt. No source documents the gear, so this tone follows the style of the record.

recipes.tips: Channel A for the chorus chords, channel B for the solo. Stomp the Tube OD for the solo if it needs more sustain. For a fatter solo, push the tone knob back in (humbucker).
recipes.why: Big modern-country choruses use a Plexi-style crunch on a Tele: bright and biting, not saturated. A quiet delay and a small room keep it tight under the vocals.
